title: Measurement validation in organizational research: evidence beyond a reliability coefficient
question: How often do adaptation/validation studies of widely used work measures (e.g. UWES, PsyCap, job insecurity) report each of the practices below, and does reporting change over the window?

documents.text:
# Measurement validation in organizational research: evidence beyond a reliability coefficient

Methodological review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

Which forms of validity evidence support using an organizational measure in a new population?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)). Written as a methodological review with a meta-research protocol.

## Evidence base and method

The author's folder (`Paper 4 Sep 2024/References`) holds 75 PDFs. All were identified against Crossref, and none is retracted. Several carry Crossref-listed corrections, noted per record in `screening.json`. Nineteen were excluded: 17 validations outside work settings (students, children, clinical, relationships), a licence page and a duplicate. Of the 56 included:

- **5** are methods commentaries used as guidance.
- **51** are measure-validation studies. Of these, **25** adapt or re-validate an existing measure in a **new population**: a new language, country, occupation or sector. These 25 are the focus here. The other 26 develop new scales.

Each study was searched in full text for ten kinds of validity evidence (`elements.py`, `audit.json`). For the 25 adaptation studies, the key elements were judged by hand: translation procedure, content validity in the new population, measurement invariance, criterion validity and comparison with the original population.

## What the collection shows

### 1. Internal structure is near-universal; external evidence is not

Across all 51 validation studies, factor-analytic evidence (CFA/EFA/ESEM) was found in 50 and convergent or discriminant evidence (often AVE-based) in 43. These are machine-detected counts. The hand-checked picture for the 25 adaptation studies:

| Evidence for the new population (hand-verified) | Adaptation studies (of 25) |
|---|---:|
| Factor structure re-tested | essentially all |
| Translation procedure reported (back-translation or committee), where translation was needed | 11 [R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10, R11] |
| Content validity re-examined (expert panel or cognitive interviews) | 5 [R12, R6, R8, R13, R9] |
| Measurement invariance tested | 14 |
| of which across demographic groups *within* the new population only | 8 [R1, R2, R14, R5, R7, R13, R10, R15] |
| of which across countries or languages | 6 [R4, R8, R16, R17, R18, R11] |
| Criterion or predictive validity in the new population | 6 [R2, R3, R14, R7, R8, R16] |
| Results explicitly compared with the original validation | 1 [R11] |

The typical adaptation re-fits the factor model, reports reliability and AVE, and tests invariance across gender. That establishes that the measure is internally coherent *in the new sample*. It does not establish that it measures the same thing as in the population where it was validated, or that it predicts what it should there.

### 2. Invariance across gender is not invariance across populations

Most invariance tests compare men and women, or age and tenure groups, inside the new population [R1, R2, R14, R5, R7, R13, R10, R15]. Only six compare countries or languages. These are the tests that bear directly on transfer to a new population, and their results are instructive:

- A psychological-capital scale showed only "a weak measurement invariance across the three cultures". The authors note "the lack of strong invariance across cultures, which prevents a meaningful comparison of factor means across countries" [R18, PDF p1].
- An age-discrimination scale "presents scalar invariance" across Spanish-speaking countries in a 5-item version [R8, abstract].
- A work-motivation scale tested invariance "across language (French [samples 1, 2 and 3] and English [samples 4 and 5])" [R16, PDF p8], the only test in the set that includes a sample in the original language.
- A Romanian thriving scale found "a differential functioning of items 2 and 9 across age" [R10, PDF p2]. Item-level non-equivalence can hide behind acceptable overall fit.

Cross-population equivalence cannot be assumed, and in this collection it frequently fails at the scalar level. Scalar invariance is the level needed to compare means.

### 3. Criterion validity is the most often missing piece, and authors say so

Six adaptation studies tested criterion or predictive validity in the new population. One example: "Evidence largely supported convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity of the scale" [R2, PDF p1]. Several others explicitly flag its absence:

- "criterion-related validity should be established, but we were not able to do so in this contribution" [R4, PDF p21]
- "tests of its predictive validity, concurrent validity, and discriminant validity will be helpful" [R9, PDF p6]
- "we cannot examine test-retest reliability or establish longitudinal predictive vali[dity]" [R10, PDF p10]

A reliable, well-fitting measure with no demonstrated relation to outcomes in the new population supports description at most, not decisions about people.

### 4. Content validity is rarely re-examined

Only five adaptation studies re-checked whether items mean the same thing to the new population. Examples include an expert panel reviewing clarity, conciseness and readability [R13, PDF p3], and cognitive interviews testing "language and meaning of items" [R6, PDF p4]. Where items carry culturally specific meaning, such as work–family roles or age norms, this is the step most likely to reveal non-equivalence before any statistics are run.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **A reliability coefficient plus a well-fitting CFA is the floor, not the case for use.** Nearly all adaptations report it; it does not show transfer.
2. **Transfer requires cross-population invariance at the level of the intended comparison.** Scalar invariance is needed to compare means across populations. It is tested in only 6 of 25 adaptations and often not achieved [R18, R10].
3. **Criterion validity in the new population is the most frequently missing evidence** (6 of 25), often acknowledged by the authors themselves [R4, R9, R10].
4. **A minimal standard for using a measure in a new population** follows from the gaps above:
   - documented translation, if needed
   - content re-validation with the target group
   - invariance against the original or a reference population, at the level matching the intended use
   - at least one criterion relation in the new population

## Limits

- 51 validation studies from one curated folder, heavily weighted toward recent journals that publish adaptations. The counts illustrate practices; they are not field prevalence.
- Hand verification covered the 25 adaptation studies. Counts for the full 51 are machine-detected.
- Supplementary materials were not searched.

## Proposed research direction (meta-research)

The companion protocol samples adaptation studies of widely used work measures (for example UWES, PsyCap, job insecurity) across journals and years. Two coders record the evidence types above. It examines whether studies that test cross-population invariance reach different conclusions about mean differences than those that do not. No participant data are collected.

# Paper 4 — Meta-research protocol v2: Validity evidence for measures used in new populations

> **Status: PROPOSAL.** Unit of analysis = published articles; no human participants. No coding has been done and no prevalence results exist. Version 2 replaces `paper-4-sep-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Question
How often do adaptation/validation studies of widely used work measures (e.g. UWES, PsyCap, job insecurity) report each of the practices below, and does reporting change over the window?

## 2. Sampling frame
- **Frame:** adaptation/validation studies of widely used work measures (e.g. UWES, PsyCap, job insecurity). The journal list and the 5-year window are fixed in the OSF pre-registration **before** searching.
- **Retrieval:** Scopus/OpenAlex query by journal ISSN and window (query string archived); every record de-duplicated by DOI.
- **Eligibility:** screened by title/abstract, then full text, by two independent screeners; disagreements resolved by discussion; PRISMA-style flow reported.
- **Sample size:** to estimate a reporting prevalence within ±.08 (95% CI, worst case p = .50) requires **151 eligible articles**. If more are eligible, a random sample of 151 (seed archived) is coded; if fewer, all are coded and the achieved precision reported.

## 3. Coding manual (core items)
| Code | Values | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| translation procedure | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| content re-validation | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| invariance vs original/reference population | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |
| criterion validity in new population | present / absent / unclear | definition and decision rules in the coding manual (pilot on 15 articles) |

Plus descriptors: journal, year, country of data, design, sample size.

## 4. Reliability
Two coders code **83 articles** independently (≥ 20% of the sample and ≥ 83, the number needed to show κ > .60 when true κ = .80, one-sided α = .05, 80% power). Codes below κ = .60 are revised and re-coded. The remainder is single-coded with 10% spot checks.

## 5. Analysis
Prevalence with Wilson 95% CIs per code; logistic regression of each code on publication year (trend) and design; all counts are reproducible from the archived coding sheet.

## 6. Ethics
Published literature only — no human participants. An IEC **exemption** request (ICMR 2017: research on publicly available information) is filed with the AMET IEC for the record.

## 7. Open science
Pre-registration, search strings, coding manual, coding sheet and analysis script on OSF.
